artifactEvidence.excerpt: A calendar question needs a reliable date, not just a convincing sentence.
Dear Temporally Confused,

Explaining a calendar and checking today’s date are different tasks. A model can generate an answer about dates from the information it has, but the app must supply a current date or give it access to a suitable tool if you want it to check the time now.

Some products supply date information automatically. Some can use search or other tools. That still leaves room for mistakes: the answer might use the wrong time zone, carry forward an old date from the conversation or get the day-of-week calculation wrong. Saying “Are you sure?” does not supply the missing fact.

For a scheduling task, give it the confirmed date, place and time zone: “Today is Monday, 7 September 2026, in Vancouver. The meeting is on Thursday, 10 September at 2 p.m. Vancouver time. Draft an invitation using those details.” If you are converting between time zones, use a calendar or time-zone converter to confirm the result.

For a question about right now, ask the tool to check a current clock if it has access to one. If it cannot, check your device’s clock yourself. For flights, appointments and deadlines, confirm the final date against the booking or calendar before acting. Miss Jeeves would rather you checked twice than arrived on Wednesday for a Tuesday lunch.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: 8.2 — The Two Sources of "Knowledge" Based on everything you've learned so far, there are only two ways the model "knows" something when it responds to you: Source 1: Training weights (frozen, general, potentially stale) Everything the model absorbed during training (Chapters 3-5) is encoded in its weights. This includes patterns of language, general facts about the world, reasoning patterns, style — everything that was in the training data. This knowledge is frozen at the training cutoff date and never updates. Source 2: Context window (live, specific, provided right now) Everything placed into the context window for this specific request — your message, conversation history, system instructions, documents you uploaded, search results, the current date. This is live information, specific to this moment, and disappears the moment the response is complete. The model can't tell the difference. When it generates a response, it draws on both sources simultaneously. It doesn't flag "this fact comes from my training" versus "this fact comes from the document you just uploaded." It processes everything in the context window as one combined input. This distinction — training knowledge vs contextual information — is fundamental to understanding both the capabilities and limitations of these systems. 8.3 — What "Memory" Actually Means (When Companies Say It) 📼 Rewind it: Calling every saved preference "memory" is how you end up with a Burn Book full of assumptions. Ask what was actually stored, where it lives, and whether the product will retrieve it next time. The model itself has not quietly become a person who remembers you. In 2024–2026, many AI products launched "memory" features — ChatGPT's Memory, Claude's memory, and others. What are these actually doing? They're not giving the model actual memory. They're doing this: Extracting facts from your conversations ("User's name is Ali." "User prefers concise answers." "User is working on a textbook project.") Storing those facts externally — in a database, outside the model. Injecting relevant facts back into the context window each time you start a new conversation. The model still has no memory. But the application layer remembers things about you and feeds them back in each time, making it appear as if the model remembers.
